description:
Why Did Scientists Think This Star Had Alien Megastructures?

Episode 46 of a daily journey through the universe. ⭐
Tabby's star: in 2015, citizen scientists found a star whose light dropped by up to 22 percent in irregular dips. Comets? Alien megastructures? We follow the clues to the answer most astronomers accept today: dust.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 47: Next stop, the Boötes Void. A hole in the universe 330 million light-years wide.

segments.text: Why did scientists once wonder if aliens were building something around a star?

visual.query: debris disk around star artist impression NASA
visual.commons: debris disk around star artist impression NASA

segments.text: NASA's Kepler telescope stared at one patch of sky for four years, watching for tiny dips in starlight when planets pass in front of their stars.
segments.headline: Kepler watches

segments.text: Volunteers checking the data found one star that did something weird. Its light dropped, and dropped again, in strange uneven dips.

visual.query: Kepler field of view Milky Way
visual.commons: Kepler field of view Milky Way

segments.headline: Something strange

segments.text: At one point, it dimmed by twenty-two percent. A planet the size of Jupiter would block only about one percent.
Astronomer Tabetha Boyajian led the study in twenty fifteen. The star became known as Tabby's star.

visual.query: star with orbiting dust ring artist concept
visual.commons: star with orbiting dust ring artist concept

segments.headline: Tabby's star

segments.text: Ideas flew. A swarm of comets? A smashed planet? Some even asked if aliens had built giant structures around it to collect energy, called a Dyson sphere.
segments.headline: Alien megastructure?

segments.text: The internet went wild. More than a thousand people chipped in to pay for more telescope time.
The new data showed the dips were deeper in blue light than red. Solid structures would block all colors equally. Fine dust doesn't.
segments.headline: The clue: color

segments.text: So most astronomers now think clouds of dust are the cause. But where the dust comes from is still not fully explained.

segments.headline: Probably dust
